title: The wars of apostasy
hookLine: some tribes refuse zakat or follow new claimants, and Abu Bakr holds the community together

cards: Two friends are arguing, both grieving the same man. One is Umar, remembered for his strong words. The other is Abu Bakr, remembered as the gentle one.

And in this argument it is the gentle one who will not move. News has reached Medina that tribes across Arabia are pulling away. Some say they will still pray, but they will no longer pay zakat to Medina.
Others have gathered around men claiming to be prophets themselves. Umar asks: how can we fight people who say there is no god but God? Today's word names that season.

teach.b: Riddah means a turning back. The histories call this time the riddah, and the campaigns of Abu Bakr's rule the wars of the riddah. Bukhari records the argument itself.
Umar quotes the Prophet: whoever says there is no god but God has protected his life and his wealth, except by the right of it. Abu Bakr takes hold of those last words.

teach.h: PRAYER AND ZAKAT, NOT ONE WITHOUT THE OTHER.
teach.b: By God, he says, I will fight whoever separates prayer from zakat, because zakat is the right owed on wealth.
Even if they hold back a single young goat that they used to give the Messenger of God, I will fight them over it.

Then Umar says: by God, it was nothing but that I saw God had opened Abu Bakr's heart to fight, and I knew it was the truth. The man who started the argument ends it agreeing. What was being held together?
Not only a treasury. The Qur'an itself pairs them: establish the prayer, and give the zakat. To keep one and drop the other was, for Abu Bakr, to start pulling the religion apart at a seam.

The claimants who said they were prophets pulled at a different seam: the belief that the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, was the last of the prophets. The histories name some of them, Musaylimah among them.
Historians, Muslim and not, read these campaigns as a defense of the faith, as holding a young state together, or both. Sunni and Shia historians also judge some particular episodes differently.
What Bukhari keeps is quieter: a gentle man refusing to let go, and a stubborn friend who came round.

how: Muslims study the riddah as part of early Islamic history, and the exchange between Abu Bakr and Umar about prayer and zakat in Sahih al-Bukhari is often taught in lessons on zakat.

o: a tax collected each year from the wealthy
a holy war declared against foreign empires
a turning back, as tribes pulled away

p: I will not separate prayer from zakat
what he would not let them hold back

s: Umar was the one who insisted on fighting
Umar questioned it. Abu Bakr insisted, and Umar came to agree.
some tribes said they would pray but not pay zakat to Medina
that refusal is at the center of Bukhari's report.
historians all read the riddah the same way
it has been read as a defense of the faith, as holding a young state together, or both, and Sunni and Shia historians differ on some episodes.

games.q: you're Umar. tribes still say there is no god but God, but refuse zakat. Abu Bakr wants to fight. you've argued. what happens next?
o: you come to agree with Abu Bakr.
you persuade Abu Bakr to let them be.
games.why: Bukhari reports Umar said he saw God had opened Abu Bakr's heart to it, and he knew it was the truth.

practice: Think of one thing you've promised, to God, to a person, or to yourself, that has started to feel heavy: a daily prayer, a weekly call, a gift you give.
Notice the voice that says, drop this one part and keep the rest, and without arguing, hold the whole promise together in your mind.

wordCard.voice: Riddah. A turning back: the name the histories give to the tribes' pulling away after the Prophet's death, and to Abu Bakr's campaigns to hold the community together. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: a turning back; the name for the tribes' pulling away after the Prophet's death.

carryVoice: Your line: holding together. Prayer and zakat, side by side. Day eight hundred sixty-nine, and counting.

sources.ref: Sahih al-Bukhari 1399–1400 (Abu Bakr and Umar on fighting those who withhold zakat)
Qur'an 2:43 (establish the prayer and give the zakat)
al-Tabari, Tarikh al-Rusul wa al-Muluk (the riddah campaigns; Musaylimah and other claimants)
